question: When Gaussian data have trace-class power-law covariance eigenvalues lambda_j(H) asymptotic to j^(-alpha), does a finite-width Gaussian random projection followed by an entrywise monomial preserve that spectral exponent, and which proof ingredients and scope restrictions determine the answer?

key_findings.claim: For a single Gaussian random-feature layer with monomial degree p, the paper proves matching eigenvalue bounds through almost all of the width: lambda_j is asymptotic, up to constants, to (log^(p-1)(j+1)/j)^alpha for 1 <= j <= c d log^(-(p+1))(d).
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 assumes alpha > 1, x ~ N(0,H), v >= d, an alpha-power-law spectrum for H, i.i.d. standard-Gaussian W, and f(y)=y^p. With probability 1-O(log^(-4)d), it sandwiches every eigenvalue in the stated index range between constants depending only on alpha and p. Thus the polynomial exponent alpha is preserved there, while the nonlinearity contributes a degree-dependent logarithmic correction.

key_findings.claim: The headline phrase that the exponent is inherited 'exactly' needs a range qualification: outside c d log^(-(p+1))(d), the theorem gives only polylogarithmically separated bounds rather than the same matching formula.
key_findings.evidence: For the remaining indices, Theorem 1 bounds lambda_j below by (j^(-1) log^(-2)(j+1))^alpha and above by (j^(-1) log^(2p)(j+1))^alpha, plus a least-eigenvalue lower bound of order (log^(p-1)d/d)^alpha. The paper itself lists removing this polylogarithmic gap as an open covariance-estimation problem. The result preserves the polynomial exponent but is not a sharp constant-or-log characterization for every eigenvalue.

key_findings.claim: The nonlinear proof isolates an all-distinct, degree-p Wick-chaos principal term whose ordered-product covariance has the claimed logarithmic spectrum; all other pairings are positive-semidefinite subleading terms with no slower decay.
key_findings.evidence: Isserlis' theorem expands each covariance entry over pairings, and compositions of cross-pair counts convert the result into a finite sum of PSD Gram matrices. The all-ones composition produces H_(1,...,1), whose ordered products of p input eigenvalues have counting function j governed by lattice-point asymptotics, yielding the log^(p-1) correction. Feynman-diagram/Wick decompositions decorrelate lower-order Gaussian products; their effective exponents are bounded above by the principal term. A dyadic head-tail decomposition and heavy-tailed matrix concentration then transfer population-product eigenvalues through the finite Gaussian sketch.

key_findings.claim: In the linear case p=1, power-law preservation is proved under substantially broader sketch distributions, but sharply only for the first order d/log d eigenvalues.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2 replaces Gaussian W with independent centered isotropic columns satisfying uniform quadratic-form moment bounds and proves lambda_j(d^(-1) W^T H W) asymptotic to j^(-alpha) for j <= c d/log d with probability 1-O(log^(-4)d). Its dyadic proof controls the leading covariance block in Loewner order and sums operator-norm bounds for the spectral tail.

key_findings.claim: Finite-width simulations support the monomial theorem for degrees one through six, but they are slope illustrations rather than quantitative finite-sample validation of the theorem's probability and constant bounds.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 2 reports normalized median post-activation eigenvalues across 100 independent Gaussian trials at alpha=1.31, v=d=10,000, and 100,000 Monte Carlo samples. Curves for p=1,...,6 track a j^(-alpha) reference with modest degree-dependent shape changes. No confidence bands, fitted exponents, coverage frequency for the two-sided theorem, or finite-d scaling analysis are reported. The surrounding prose says v=d=m=10,000 whereas the caption says m=100,000, leaving the Monte Carlo sample count internally inconsistent.

key_findings.claim: Power-law-looking spectra extend empirically to several non-Gaussian data sources and non-monomial activations, but one tested smooth activation, z^2 exp(-z^2), is an explicit counterexample to broad activation universality.
key_findings.evidence: At alpha=1.31, d=3,000, and 30,000 samples, Gaussian, Rademacher, Student-t(4), and covariance-shaped CIFAR-10 curves have similar slopes across the tested activations. ReLU, tanh, and Heaviside also track the reference in Figure 2. In contrast, z^2 exp(-z^2) deviates strongly; the authors note that summing degree-dependent logarithmic corrections can yield non-power-law decay or altered exponents for some analytic activations. None of these beyond-monomial or beyond-Gaussian observations is covered by Theorem 1.

key_findings.claim: CIFAR-10 experiments show recognizable power laws across depth, but material slope drift means multilayer 'preservation' is qualitative rather than equality of exponents.
key_findings.evidence: Using 10,000 images and OLS fits over eigenvalue ranks 1-100, every reported layer has R^2 above 0.875. A random tanh MLP stays near -1.28 from an input slope -1.29, while random ReLU flattens to -0.95 and random He3 to -0.83; LayerNorm accelerates flattening to -0.75. Random ResNet-20 is comparatively stable (-1.17 to -1.25), whereas trained networks flatten sharply in middle layers and steepen late. These observations are consistent with, but do not establish, accumulated logarithmic corrections.

anchors.section: Appendix E Power-law persistence across layers

key_findings.claim: Appendix E contains a direct numeric contradiction about the trained ResNet-20 final-layer slope.
key_findings.evidence: The body text, Appendix E prose, Table 1, and Figure 11 label G3-B3 as -1.35 versus the -1.29 input. Figure 12's caption instead says the same trained ResNet-20 final layer has slope -1.29 and matches the input, even though the plotted annotation on that page reads 1.35 in magnitude. The defensible statement is approximate recovery, not exact matching.

key_findings.claim: The work establishes a covariance-spectrum building block, not a neural scaling law or a random-feature regression risk theorem.
key_findings.evidence: The analyzed object is the population covariance over Gaussian inputs conditional on one finite random sketch. Targets, labels, optimization, empirical training samples, ridge parameters, and test error do not appear in Theorem 1. The authors explicitly list combining the spectral result with random-feature ridge-regression analysis as future work. Therefore any claimed improvement or prediction of parameter/data/compute scaling exponents is downstream conjecture.

anchors.section: Open questions / Test error under power-law data

method.core_idea: Express the covariance of monomial random features as a finite positive-semidefinite sum of Gaussian-chaos Gram matrices, identify the all-distinct degree-p chaos as the spectral principal term, count the products of power-law input eigenvalues, and prove that a finite Gaussian sketch preserves those product spectra up to a nearly full-width cutoff.
method.mechanism: After rotating H to diagonal form and writing x=sqrt(H)z, Isserlis' theorem expands E[(w_i^T x)^p(w_j^T x)^p] over pairings. Cross-pair counts and integer compositions yield PSD terms d^(-1) D^A Y_pi^T Y_pi D^A. The all-cross, all-ones composition has diagonal population covariance indexed by strictly ordered p-tuples with eigenvalues proportional to products H_i1...H_ip; Tauberian and dyadic lattice-point counting order these products as (log^(p-1)(j+1)/j)^alpha. Nonprincipal products are transformed into orthogonal Wick matrices through Feynman-diagram decompositions and shown to decay at least as fast. For each term, a dyadic spectral head-tail split combines matrix concentration for heavy-tailed Gaussian-polynomial columns, hypercontractivity, and a smallest-singular-value bound to control the finite-width Gram matrix. Experiments then probe monomial degree, non-monomial activations, non-Gaussian data, and multiple neural architectures beyond the theorem.
assumptions: The input is exactly Gaussian, x ~ N(0,H), for the nonlinear theorem.
The covariance has two-sided alpha-power-law eigenvalues with alpha > 1, so its spectrum is summable.
The input dimension satisfies v >= d and the nonlinear sketch W has i.i.d. standard-Gaussian entries.
The activation is the integer monomial f(y)=y^p; sums or infinite Hermite expansions are not controlled by Theorem 1.
The result concerns one random layer and the population covariance over x, conditional on W.
Constants hidden by asymptotic notation may depend on alpha and p but not on d or v.
The eigenvalue ordering of product covariances is captured by asymptotic lattice-point counts, with finite-v truncation controlled only in the required index range.
Gaussian hypercontractivity and finite polynomial degree provide enough tail control for a d/log^(p+1)d covariance head, but not a sharp full-spectrum estimate.
The empirical CIFAR, non-Gaussian, general-activation, trained-network, and multilayer results are exploratory rather than consequences of the theorem.

techniques.role: Converts degree-2p Gaussian moments into a finite sum indexed by pairings and cross-pair compositions.
Represents the full covariance as a sum of PSD Gram matrices, enabling termwise spectral upper bounds and a principal-term lower bound.
Orders products of power-law eigenvalues and derives the log^(p-1) correction with Tauberian and dyadic counting arguments.
Projects correlated Gaussian products into homogeneous Wick chaoses with diagonal row covariance.
Concentrates a leading spectral block and controls all later blocks by summable operator-norm bounds.
Handles empirical covariance matrices whose Gaussian-polynomial columns are not sub-Gaussian.
Supplies stretched-exponential tails and moments for degree-p and degree-2p chaos variables.
Provides a lower bound on the least eigenvalue from independent isotropic polynomial rows.
Tests how far the spectral pattern extends beyond monomials and Gaussian inputs.
Fits ranks 1-100 of layer activation covariances in MLP, CNN, and ResNet models before and after training.

evaluations.setting: Gaussian alpha=1.31 covariance, monomials p=1,...,6, v=d=10,000, median over 100 independent sketches; Figure 2 caption reports 100,000 Monte Carlo samples
evaluations.metric: Normalized random-feature covariance eigenvalue curves on log-log axes
evaluations.result: All six monomial curves show the predicted polynomial slope with modest degree-dependent curvature/log shifts
evaluations.baseline: Input reference j^(-1.31); no fitted-slope errors or theorem-coverage frequencies

evaluations.setting: Same Gaussian construction with ReLU, tanh, Heaviside, and z^2 exp(-z^2)
evaluations.result: ReLU, tanh, and Heaviside look power-law-like, while z^2 exp(-z^2) deviates strongly

evaluations.setting: Gaussian, Rademacher, Student-t(4), and CIFAR-10 inputs shaped to alpha=1.31, d=3,000, 30,000 samples, six activations
evaluations.metric: Cross-distribution normalized spectral slope and shape
evaluations.result: For each activation, the four data-source curves have broadly consistent slopes; p=2 and p=3 also track the paper's composition-count prediction
evaluations.baseline: Gaussian theory and zero-free-parameter p=2/p=3 lattice-count curves

evaluations.setting: 10,000 CIFAR-10 images through four-layer width-1024 random MLPs
evaluations.metric: OLS slope and R^2 over covariance eigenvalue ranks 1-100
evaluations.result: Input -1.29; tanh ends -1.28, ReLU -0.95, He3 -0.83; every reported MLP fit has R^2 above 0.989

evaluations.setting: Random four-layer ReLU MLP with no normalization, RMSNorm, or LayerNorm
evaluations.result: No norm -0.95, RMSNorm -0.85, LayerNorm -0.75, so normalization increases flattening

evaluations.setting: Random and trained VGG-style four-block CNN on CIFAR-10; trained CNN reaches 86.2% test accuracy
Random and trained CIFAR ResNet-20 across Conv1 and nine residual blocks
evaluations.metric: Per-block covariance slopes and R^2 over ranks 1-100
evaluations.result: Random residual blocks stay between -1.17 and -1.25; trained blocks flatten to -0.52 early and reach -1.35 at G3-B3, with R^2 above 0.875
evaluations.baseline: Input slope -1.29; Figure 12 caption inconsistently calls the final trained slope -1.29

limitations: Author-acknowledged: the theorem covers monomials, not polynomials, ReLU, tanh, sigmoid, or general Hermite expansions.
Author-acknowledged: sharp matching bounds stop at c d log^(-(p+1))(d); the remaining eigenvalues retain a large polylogarithmic gap.
Author-acknowledged: universality beyond Gaussian W is proved only for p=1, while the nonlinear theorem requires Gaussian sketches.
Author-acknowledged: converting the covariance result into random-feature ridge-regression test-error scaling laws is future work.

Reviewer-identified: Theorem 1 assumes Gaussian inputs, alpha > 1, v >= d, a single layer, and an exact monomial; it does not formally support the broad language about real data, classical activations, depth, convolution, residual connections, normalization, or training.
Reviewer-identified: preserving a polynomial eigenvalue exponent with degree-dependent logarithms is weaker than preserving the full spectrum or exact finite-rank slopes.
Reviewer-identified: z^2 exp(-z^2) is a tested exception, so activation universality is false without substantive regularity and coefficient conditions.

Reviewer-identified: the experiments normalize by the top eigenvalue and mostly show curves; they do not report fitted confidence intervals, finite-size rates, constants, or empirical coverage of the high-probability theorem.
Reviewer-identified: Figure 2's prose and caption disagree on whether the Monte Carlo sample count is 10,000 or 100,000.

Reviewer-identified: multilayer experiments show large exponent drift, especially with He3 and normalization, so 'preservation across layers' means continued approximate power-law form rather than an unchanged exponent.
Reviewer-identified: covariance fits use only ranks 1-100 from 10,000 CIFAR images, leaving bulk/tail behavior, sample-covariance bias, and alternative fit ranges untested.
Reviewer-identified: only CIFAR-10 is used for the deep-network study, and seed counts or uncertainty across initializations/training runs are not reported.
Reviewer-identified: the ResNet-20 final-layer value is -1.35 in text, Table 1, and the plotted annotation but -1.29 in Figure 12's caption.

Reviewer-identified: the theoretical covariance is uncentered E[f(W^T x)f(W^T x)^T]/d, whereas Appendix E explicitly centers empirical activations; even-degree monomials can make this distinction material through a mean/rank-one term.
Reviewer-identified: no labels, targets, optimization dynamics, empirical kernel matrix, or prediction risk enter the main theorem, so connections to neural scaling laws remain indirect.
Reviewer-identified: hidden constants depend on degree p, and the paper does not study regimes where p grows with width or depth.
failure_modes: An activation whose Hermite components cancel, interact, or extend to unbounded degree can change the exponent or destroy a clean power law, as the z^2 exp(-z^2) experiment suggests.
Repeated layers can accumulate logarithmic corrections until finite-range fitted slopes drift substantially from the input slope.
LayerNorm or RMSNorm can flatten the spectrum faster than the unnormalized random-feature heuristic predicts.
For alpha <= 1, the trace-class and summability arguments used to control spectral tails no longer apply.
Heavy-tailed or dependent sketch entries may violate the polynomial-chaos concentration needed for a nearly full-width head block.
Finite sample covariance can make spectral tails peel off because rank is limited by the number of observations, even when the population law persists.
Even-degree activations introduce mean/rank-one components that can dominate top eigenvalues if centered and uncentered covariances are conflated.
Training and residual connections can reshape rather than merely transmit spectra, so iterating the one-layer theorem with fresh independent weights is not a model of a trained network.
Large monomial degree increases both the log correction and the cutoff penalty log^(p+1)d, reducing the fraction with sharp finite-width guarantees.
A power-law covariance alone does not determine learning curves when target alignment, noise, regularization, or optimizer dynamics differ.
reusable_insights: For products of p trace-class power-law sequences, multiplicative lattice counts naturally produce a log^(p-1) correction without changing the polynomial exponent.
A PSD chaos decomposition is especially useful for spectral proofs because one principal term can certify a lower bound while every term can be bounded separately above.
Wick projection can convert correlated Gaussian-product rows into orthogonal chaos coordinates with diagonal covariance.
When sample-covariance columns are polynomial Gaussian chaoses rather than sub-Gaussian, a dyadic spectral split can localize concentration to the effective head dimension.
Separate preservation of power-law form, preservation of polynomial exponent, and preservation of exact fitted slope; they are materially different claims.
Test candidate activations for leading Hermite degree, coefficient cancellation, and infinite-degree accumulation before extrapolating monomial theory.
Use skip connections and normalization as explicit spectral interventions: the former can anchor an input spectrum, while the latter can whiten or flatten it.
Keep centered versus uncentered covariance conventions explicit when nonlinear features have nonzero means.
open_questions: Which necessary and sufficient conditions on Hermite coefficients make a general activation preserve the input's polynomial spectral exponent?
Can robust covariance estimation or small-ball methods remove the log^(p+1)d cutoff and give matching bounds for all d eigenvalues?
Does nonlinear power-law preservation hold for non-Gaussian sketches under moment matching, and how heavy may the tails be?
Can the result be extended to alpha <= 1 with dimension-dependent normalization or nonsummable spectra?
How do correlations between weights across trained layers change the multiplicative log corrections?
Can one derive random-feature ridge-regression excess-risk and compute/data/parameter scaling laws directly from this finite-width spectrum?
Do empirical activation covariances on larger vision and language datasets retain the same behavior after controlling sample size and fit range?
Why do normalization layers accelerate spectral flattening, and can that effect be predicted analytically?
Does training deliberately restore task-relevant spectral directions, or is the late-layer steepening a finite-sample or architecture artifact?
Which of -1.35 or -1.29 is the intended trained ResNet-20 final-layer estimate, and do independent reruns reproduce it?

competitive_landscape.title: Kernel ridge regression under power-law data: spectrum and generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Wortsman and Loureiro derive the spectrum of polynomial inner-product kernel integral operators under anisotropic Gaussian power-law data and show that for alpha>1 the operator spectrum has the same capacity exponent. That already contains the core polynomial-kernel inheritance phenomenon at the infinite population-operator level. The present paper instead proves high-probability finite-width eigenvalue bounds for the random d-by-d feature covariance conditional on a Gaussian sketch, including its explicit log correction and sketch tail; it does not provide the predecessor's KRR generalization theorem.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws in Linear Regression: Compute, Parameters, and Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Lin et al. analyze one-pass SGD on linearly sketched covariates with power-law covariance and derive parameter/data risk exponents. Their spectral input is the p=1 sketched covariance and their goal is learning-curve theory. The present paper extends finite-sketch spectral preservation to monomials but stops before an SGD or test-risk analysis.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2024 official proceedings, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37

competitive_landscape.title: On the Spectrum of Random Features Maps of High Dimensional Data
competitive_landscape.difference: Liao and Couillet study limiting empirical Gram spectra of nonlinear random feature maps for high-dimensional Gaussian-mixture data. They characterize how activation moments and class structure enter the random matrix, but not ordered eigenvalue decay inherited from a trace-class power-law population covariance. The present paper studies a population-over-input d-by-d covariance at finite width and gives per-eigenvalue high-probability bounds.
competitive_landscape.source_version: PMLR volume 80, ICML 2018 official paper (10-15 July 2018)

competitive_landscape.title: Dimension-free deterministic equivalents and scaling laws for random feature regression
competitive_landscape.difference: Defilippis, Loureiro, and Misiakiewicz give non-asymptotic dimension-free deterministic equivalents for random-feature ridge-regression error and derive sharp rates when the feature-map spectrum and target decay satisfy power laws. They largely assume or abstract the relevant feature eigenvalues; the present paper derives those eigenvalues from a specific anisotropic Gaussian input plus monomial sketch but does not close the risk analysis.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2024 official proceedings, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37

competitive_landscape.title: Asymptotics of Learning with Deep Structured (Random) Features
competitive_landscape.relationship: deep random-feature covariance and learning predecessor
competitive_landscape.difference: Schroder et al. derive population-feature covariance formulas and high-dimensional readout test error for broad deep structured random features under proportional asymptotics. Their scope includes depth and structured weights, but not ordered power-law eigenvalue bounds or the log correction for trace-class anisotropic inputs. The present paper is sharper on that narrow spectrum question and only experimental on depth.
competitive_landscape.source_version: PMLR volume 235, ICML 2024 official paper (21-27 July 2024)

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims the first finite-width characterization showing that a nonlinear random-feature layer with monomial activation inherits an alpha-power-law input covariance exponent, with matching bounds for almost all feature eigenvalues and only a degree-dependent logarithmic correction.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Theorem 1 gives two-sided high-probability bounds through c d log^(-(p+1))(d); the proof combines a principal Wick-chaos product spectrum, lattice counts, and finite-sketch concentration. Theorem 2 recovers and broadens the linear sketch case, and experiments explore activations, inputs, and depth outside the theorem.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The narrow defensible novelty is the finite-width, conditional-on-random-sketch, per-eigenvalue theorem for monomial features and its explicit logarithmic correction. The claimed inheritance combination is not wholly new: Wortsman and Loureiro already derive power-law inheritance for polynomial kernel integral operators, linear sketches were already analyzed in scaling-law work, and random-feature risk theory already uses power-law feature spectra. The paper is complementary because finite sketch randomness is absent from the closest operator result. General nonlinear activations, non-Gaussian inputs, multiple layers, trained networks, and scaling-law/test-error consequences remain empirical or open, and the tail is only polylogarithmically sharp.

reviewer_notes: The full 46-page arXiv v1 PDF was read end to end, including the concentration, Wick-product, lattice-counting, eigenvalue, and CIFAR-10 appendices. A second passage rechecked Theorems 1-2, Propositions 1-2, the Figure 2 settings, Appendix E Table 1, and Figures 11-12 against the PDF. Five primary competitor records were checked through arXiv or official NeurIPS/PMLR proceedings using mechanism/task, closest-baseline/evaluation, and claimed-novelty/predecessor query families. Residual uncertainty is confined to experiments: Figure 2 conflicts on 10,000 versus 100,000 Monte Carlo samples, Appendix E conflicts on -1.35 versus -1.29 for the trained ResNet final layer, and no raw data or reruns were available. The theorem statements and proof scope are otherwise clear.

verification.passage_check: Secondary passage checked every body and appendix page; theorem ranges, probability, assumptions, principal/subleading decomposition, experimental settings, and the two internal numeric contradictions were rechecked directly in the 46-page PDF.
verification.competitor_check: Primary-source audit checked Wortsman-Loureiro arXiv v1, Lin et al. NeurIPS 2024, Liao-Couillet ICML 2018, Defilippis et al. NeurIPS 2024, and Schroder et al. ICML 2024; the audit confirms prior operator-level polynomial power-law inheritance and narrows novelty to finite-width monomial covariance bounds.
